title: Manhattan Project
summary: The Manhattan Project was the secret World War II program directed by the United States Army Corps of Engineers and leading scientists that developed the first nuclear weapons, culminating in the Trinity test and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.
card: Initiated under military command in August 1942 following warnings from Albert Einstein and Leo Szilard, the project mobilized roughly 130,000 workers and approximately $2 billion to produce fissile materials at Oak Ridge and Hanford. Under scientific director J. Robert Oppenheimer at Los Alamos, physicists designed and assembled both uranium gun-type and plutonium implosion weapons. The successful Trinity detonation on July 16, 1945, proved the implosion design, enabling the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki that brought World War II to an end while launching the nuclear age.
what:
The Manhattan Project was the covert Anglo-American program that developed the world's first nuclear weapons between 1942 and 1945. Prompted by the August 1939 Einstein–Szilárd letter warning President Franklin D. Roosevelt of potential German atomic weapons research, and accelerated by the British MAUD Committee report of July 1941, the United States Army Corps of Engineers formally established the Manhattan Engineer District on August 13, 1942, under Colonel James C. Marshall, followed in September by the appointment of Brigadier General Leslie R. Groves as overall director.

Scientific momentum surged on December 2, 1942, when Enrico Fermi's team achieved the first controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in Chicago Pile-1 at the University of Chicago. To produce sufficient weapons-grade fissile material, the military built sprawling secret industrial complexes: the Clinton Engineer Works at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, which separated uranium-235 using electromagnetic and gaseous diffusion plants, and the Hanford Engineer Works in Washington State, where industrial reactors irradiated natural uranium to manufacture plutonium-239. Raw uranium came predominantly from the high-grade Shinkolobwe mine in the Belgian Congo, alongside Canadian pitchblende and western domestic ores. Weapon design and assembly were centralized at Project Y on the Pajarito Plateau in Los Alamos, New Mexico, directed by theoretical physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer.

The project culminated in the Trinity test on July 16, 1945, in New Mexico's Jornada del Muerto desert, successfully detonating an implosion plutonium weapon yielding approximately twenty kilotons of TNT. Three weeks later, the United States detonated the Little Boy uranium bomb over Hiroshima on August 6 and the Fat Man plutonium bomb over Nagasaki on August 9, prompting Japan's surrender on August 15, 1945. Estimates of cumulative financial cost range from roughly $1.9 billion in then-year expenditures tabulated by historians Richard Hewlett and Oscar Anderson to $2.2 billion cited by Department of Energy records, reflecting different accounting cutoffs between wartime activity and the 1947 civilian transition.

uncertainty.note: Start is the official establishment of the Manhattan Engineer District on 13 August 1942; precursor research dates to the Einstein-Szilárd letter of 2 August 1939 and the MAUD report of July 1941. End marks the announcement of Japan's surrender on 15 August 1945; operations transferred to the civilian Atomic Energy Commission on 1 January 1947.

how: The Manhattan Project succeeded through a parallel, dual-track industrial strategy combining fundamental physics, rapid chemical engineering, and unprecedented military-industrial mobilization. Because physicists were uncertain whether electromagnetic separation, gaseous diffusion, or thermal diffusion would yield sufficient uranium-235, Groves funded all three processes simultaneously at Oak Ridge. Concurrently, theoretical calculations showed that reactor-bred element 94 (plutonium) could be chemically separated from irradiated uranium far faster than isotope enrichment, prompting the construction of water-cooled production reactors along the Columbia River at Hanford. When Los Alamos researchers discovered in 1944 that spontaneous fission in plutonium-240 precluded using a simple gun-assembly mechanism for plutonium, Oppenheimer reorganized the laboratory to master explosive implosion—using shaped high-explosive lenses to compress a subcritical plutonium pit into a supercritical mass in microseconds. This vast enterprise required recruiting over 125,000 industrial and construction personnel, procuring rich pitchblende ore from the Belgian Congo's Shinkolobwe mine, and maintaining extreme compartmentalized secrecy across dozens of university laboratories and corporate contractors, including DuPont, Tennessee Eastman, and Stone & Webster.
why_it_matters:
The Manhattan Project fundamentally reorganized global geopolitics, military strategy, and scientific research. By producing the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, it brought World War II to an immediate conclusion and ushered in the nuclear age. The demonstration of atomic energy initiated a forty-year Cold War nuclear arms race between the United States and the Soviet Union, defined by the doctrine of mutually assured destruction and global proliferation concerns that persist today. Institutionally, the project established the model for modern 'big science'—large-scale state-funded partnerships between federal agencies, research universities, and private corporations that evolved directly into the United States national laboratory system.

The project also left enduring human and environmental costs. Downwind civilian communities exposed to fallout from the Trinity detonation in New Mexico's Tularosa Basin suffered elevated rates of cancer and chronic illnesses without early notification or medical assistance. Indigenous nations, including the Wanapum, Yakama, Nez Perce, and Umatilla at Hanford, and Pueblo communities surrounding Los Alamos, suffered displacement and long-term radiological contamination of traditional ancestral hunting, fishing, and ceremonial grounds. Had the project failed to achieve a working weapon before the war's conclusion, the United States military would have executed Operation Downfall, a massive conventional amphibious invasion of the Japanese home islands that military planners projected would cause catastrophic casualties on both sides; conversely, without the wartime race to preempt Nazi Germany, international development of atomic energy might have proceeded under open civilian auspices rather than military secrecy.

related.because: The Manhattan Project developed, engineered, and delivered the uranium-235 gun-type weapon Little Boy that was detonated over Hiroshima on 6 August 1945.
The Manhattan Project produced the plutonium-239 implosion weapon Fat Man that was detonated over Nagasaki on 9 August 1945.

beats.caption: Following the 1939 Einstein-Szilard letter, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers establishes the Manhattan Engineer District in New York City.
Enrico Fermi's team at the University of Chicago achieves the world's first controlled nuclear chain reaction in Chicago Pile-1.
Massive industrial production begins at Oak Ridge to enrich uranium-235, while Hanford constructs reactors to produce plutonium-239.
At Los Alamos, Oppenheimer coordinates weapons physics and implosion engineering, leading to the successful Trinity test in southern New Mexico.
Fissile materials shipped to Tinian enable atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, forcing Japan's surrender and inaugurating the global nuclear arms race.

perspectives.holder: United States military and political leadership (President Harry S. Truman, Secretary of War Henry Stimson, and General Leslie Groves)
perspectives.account: Argued that the rapid completion and operational deployment of atomic bombs against Hiroshima and Nagasaki was a military necessity to secure unconditional Japanese surrender without an Allied amphibious invasion (Operation Downfall), thereby saving an estimated hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives and shortening World War II.

perspectives.holder: Dissenting Manhattan Project scientists (Leo Szilard, James Franck, and signatories of the Franck Report and Szilard Petition)
perspectives.account: Argued against the unannounced combat use of atomic weapons against civilian population centers, urging a prior non-combat technical demonstration before international observers or an explicit surrender ultimatum, warning that unilateral military detonation would initiate an unconstrained global nuclear arms race with the Soviet Union.

perspectives.holder: Displaced Indigenous nations (Wanapum, Yakama, Nez Perce, Umatilla, and Rio Grande Pueblos) and New Mexico downwinder advocacy groups
perspectives.account: Argue that the project was conducted with disregard for local populations, resulting in the uncompensated seizure of sacred treaty lands, long-term environmental contamination of the Columbia River and regional watersheds, and elevated cancer mortality among Downwinders who consumed fallout-irradiated water, milk, and crops.

numbers.note: Documented by historians Richard Hewlett and Oscar Anderson and published by the Brookings Institution; total capital and operating expenditures through 1945 amounted to $1,889,604,000 in then-year dollars (equivalent to $21,570,821,000 in constant 1996 dollars).

numbers.label: Total wartime Manhattan Project expenditure reported by the Department of Energy
numbers.note: Official Department of Energy historical overview states that by the end of the war, the project had spent $2.2 billion.

numbers.label: Peak total project workforce employed across all facilities (June 1944)
numbers.note: Office of Scientific and Technical Information records state peak employment reached nearly 129,000 in June 1944; broader Department of Energy overviews cite approximately 130,000 workers at peak.

numbers.label: Total construction personnel hired through the end of 1946
numbers.note: Department of Energy records indicate over 360,000 construction workers were hired in total by end of 1946, with roughly 220,000 at Oak Ridge and 130,000 at Hanford.

numbers.label: Peak construction workforce employed on project sites (June 1944)
numbers.note: Of nearly 129,000 total personnel employed at the June 1944 peak, 84,500 were construction workers.

audience_note: Contains historical discussion of nuclear warfare, catastrophic civilian casualties from the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, radioactive fallout exposure affecting civilian downwinder populations, and the forced displacement of Indigenous and local communities.

importance.justification: Developed the first nuclear weapons, ending World War II and initiating the global nuclear age and Cold War arms race.

reviewer_note: Least certain of the precise portion of early Congolese pitchblende processed specifically into Little Boy versus Hanford reactor targets, as wartime inventory accounting aggregated Shinkolobwe and Canadian feedstocks after refinery blending.
parent_reconciliation: Manhattan Project expenditures of roughly $1.9 to $2.2 billion formed part of total United States World War II defense expenditures of approximately $3.3 trillion (under 1 percent of overall American wartime spending). Personnel mobilized peaked at nearly 130,000 workers within an Allied wartime military and industrial mobilization exceeding 16 million Americans.
